newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS -Brazil stock sell-off spotlights weaknesses.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS -Brazil stock sell-off spotlights weaknesses.

text.p: Brazilian fundamentals may not have warranted the lashing its stock market and Brady bonds were dealt this week, but economists say the frantic sell-off spotlights the shortcomings of the nation's economic program.

While economists believe government assurances that no steep devaluation is in the works -- as was widely rumored in Latin American bourses Tuesday -- they say the market battering underlines the need to rein in public spending and slow the widening current account gap.
"This should make the government more aware of its limits. I think it will be more concerned about the current account deficit," said Carlos Kawall, Citibank's chief Brazil economist.
Brazilian stocks were up over 80 percent on the year prior to this week's sell-off, which shaved 12 percent off the nation's leading Bovespa stock index on Monday and Tuesday.
The market bounced back Wednesday on rumors of heavy buying by the National Development Bank (BNDES).

Profit-taking on Monday and Tuesday was blamed on currency fears stemming from recent Asian devaluations that began with Thailand earlier this month. Because Brazil shares many of Thailand's macroeconomic woes -- high trade and current account deficits and a perceived overvalued currency -- the market drew up a quick contagion scenario.

Brazil has pointed out that its current account deficit -- at 4.2 percent of gross domestic product -- is nowhere near the critical seven-to-eight percent levels reached by Thailand this month and Mexico ahead of its 1994 peso crisis.
Officials also add that nearly half of the current account deficit is financed by foreign direct investment, a much sounder alternative to the short-term capital flows on which Mexico had relied.
But economists say Brazil has lessons to learn from Asia's recent currency turmoil.

"Thailand was seen as the benchmark to support the argument that countries could run a six to seven percent of GDP current account deficit as long as they were financing it with foreign direct investment. This benchmark has been broken," said Marcelo Allain, chief economist at Brazilian bank BMC.

Economists say Brazil's current account gap -- fueled by record trade deficits over the past two years -- will get worse before it gets better. They add the real test of Brazil's three-year stabilization drive will come in the next two years.
"If the current account deficit hits five percent of GDP, as we see it next year, then that is the kind of number that gets very uncomfortable," Citibank's Kawall said.
Brasilia has held its ground amid the market volatility, pledging no change in the foreign exchange regime and blaming the sell-off on profit-taking in an over-bought market.
President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, dismissing comparisons with the Asian "tiger" countries, said: "We do not leap like cats. We are a whale which moves slowly, but with firmness."
While analysts acknowledge Brazilian fundamentals are not rock-solid, they say the country is on sure enough footing to resist any speculative strike on the real.
Brazil has much more room to raise interest rates than Thailand or the Philippines. It also has $59 billion in U.S. dollar reserves, which it would not hesitate to use to support a tumbling real.

Prior to the sell-off, economists did not expect a serious devaluation -- 15-20 percent -- until after the October 1998 presidential election. This week's events do not change that scenario, they said.

"It's not that we're not concerned about Brazilian fundamentals. But with good international liquidity and favorable global interest rates the Brazilian situation is financeable," said Geraldo Carbone, BankBoston's president in Brazil.
"We are hardly on the verge of a crisis," Carbone said.
((-- Sao Paulo newsroom, 5511 248-5414)
